name: spy-swagger
idea: 1960s spy swagger: Twangy baritone guitar, walking bass, brass stabs, vibraphone: the cool-crew walk. The 39p lands on a big brass chord that slides down like a sad trombone; the jar gets the strings swelling back up. Why it fits: The swagger is built in, and its self-aware glamour is made for ridicule: the grander it sounds, the smaller the frog. What it risks: The obvious pick. Suno drifts towards one famous spy theme, which the parody rule forbids; it must stay generic. Its 'hope' is grand rather than warm.

name: hard-funk
idea: Hard funk groove: A locked one-chord groove on the one: chicken-scratch guitar, slapped bass, horn stabs cut to every move (the tap, the step, the duck). The groove stops dead on 39p (needle off); it drops back in, brighter, on the jar. Why it fits: The library names it for heists and comic swagger; a loop that never changes is the cleanest bed under a few spoken lines, and a dead stop is the best sting. What it risks: Can feel like a period pastiche with no modern edge; little room for warmth, so the hope has to come from the groove returning, not from a melody.

name: library-cue
idea: British library cue: A 1970s KPM-style jazz-funk cue (Hammond, wah guitar, fuzzy bass, brass fanfare) that sounds like a TV caper from British telly. The sting on 39p is a 'tension' cue; the jar gets a 'Happy Ending' button. Why it fits: British where the heist genre is American, so it fits a corner shop and a Liverpool voice; it plays the joke as a cheap TV thriller. What it risks: Can tip into nostalgia telly and feel dated rather than slick; Jack asked for heavy heist-film swagger and this is its small-screen cousin.

name: corner-shop-break
idea: The corner-shop break (invented for this short): A modern big-beat heist groove (a dusty drum break, organ, scratched record, low strings) where the shop is part of the band: the till drawer is the snare, the coin jar the shaker, the shop-door bell the hook. On 39p the record winds down; the jar fills with coins tuned up a major chord, and the beat comes back. Why it fits: The slickest of the options, closest to the turn-of-the-century heist film Jack named, but made of the corner shop, so it's ours and never that film's score. The coins carry the way out in the sound itself. What it risks: The most work: Suno makes the groove, the shop sounds are cut in by hand on the timeline. Too many effects can muddy the spoken lines.

name: tiptoe-caper
idea: Tiptoe cartoon caper (invented for this short): Sneaking music: pizzicato strings, a muted sax and bassoon on tiptoe, every step hit on a plucked note, the laser duck a held breath. 39p gets a deflating tuba 'wah-wah'; the jar a warm clarinet lift. Why it fits: The laughiest: it says 'these lot are clowns' and lets the 39p land as a gag. The swagger becomes sneaky swagger. What it risks: Undercuts the 'played straight' brief: it tells the audience it's a joke before the twist does. The sad-trombone sting is a cliché.

name: colliery-brass
idea: Colliery brass band (against the grain): A northern brass band plays the job as a proud slow march, cornets and side drum, deadly serious. 39p: the band falters, one euphonium left. The jar: the whole band back in as a hymn, the way out sounding like a win for working people. Why it fits: The strongest 'hope' of all of them, and the most British; it reframes the crew as ordinary working people, which is the point. What it risks: The library says it undermines comedy and fast rhythm: little swagger, and the cuts can't land on fast hits. It may feel like a different film from the picture.

name: clockwork-pulse
idea: Clockwork pulse (against the grain): Ticking marimba and piano in steady eighth notes, the plan as a machine, building in layers with every clip. 39p: one wrong note and it all stops. The jar: the pulse restarts and climbs, price and savings rising together as one harmonic climb. Why it fits: The way out is a mechanism (money that keeps up), and this is the only sound that makes it one; the pulse leaves every spoken line clear. What it risks: Clever rather than swaggering: it loses the cool-crew feel Jack asked for, and minimal music can feel like an advert for a bank.
